regions.name: Labyrinth spawn lists: 3 pointers
regions.description: $89FB reads $803C,Y / $803D,Y with Y = 2 * $0478[low nibble of $04C0,X], then (pointer),Y with the high nibble for an object type. Three pointers, $AF61, $AF69, $AF71; the 6 bytes are exactly the gap between the entry table and the code at $8042. How far each list runs is NOT established - the index can reach 15 and the lists are 8 apart.

regions.name: Room shape pointer: $91EA + 18 x (A AND $1F)
regions.description: Called once, from $826B. $17:$16 := the address of room shape n, n = A AND $1F: A x 8 + A = 9 A, doubled = 18 A, plus $91EA (the 19 shapes of 18 bytes, one bit per cell, that $8278 lays into the room buffer). RUN: n = 0-31 matched $91EA + 18 n exactly (A = $23 used 3).

regions.name: Exit displacement, x: by exit code / 2
regions.description: 00 FF 00 01 00 for the exit codes N, W, none, E, S (code / 2 = 0-4): x changes by 0, -1, 0, +1, 0 ($FF added to the column byte).

regions.name: Exit displacement, y: by exit code / 2
regions.description: FF 00 00 00 01: y changes by -1, 0, 0, 0, +1. (The pair of tables is bounded by the same routine's two reads six bytes apart; the second ends on the first instruction of $8071.)

regions.name: MOVE THE POSITION (slot $802D): apply the exit to ($52, $53)
regions.description: Called by the room loaders and the game start (with $A4 = 4 for 'no move'). Y := $A4 / 2; the map column $52 += $8067,Y and the row $53 += $806C,Y; $19 := the column and $18 := the row (the targets for the seek below). RUN: all 43 (position, exit) cases tried, including every edge and corner, ended on the right cell.

regions.name: Neighbour records: start the seek at the top of the map
regions.description: The seek counters $14 (row) and $15 (column) := 0 and the walk pointer $17:$16 := $8A6E, the first world-map record.

regions.name: Neighbour pointer N ($E0/$E1)
regions.description: Unless the row is 0: seek to (row - 1, column) with $80F5 and restore the row. $E1 gets the record's high address byte and $E0 the low; for a row of 0 (no cell to the north) $E1 := 0, which marks 'none'. The five pointers are built in ONE forward walk, in raster order N, W, own, E, S, so the map is read once. The pointer table is $E0 N, $E2 W, $E4 the room itself, $E6 E, $E8 S. RUN.

regions.name: Neighbour pointer W ($E2/$E3)
regions.description: Unless the column is 0: seek on to (row, column - 1); $E3 := 0 when there is none.

regions.name: The room's own record ($E4/$E5)
regions.description: Seek on to (row, column). Every later routine reads the room through ($E4).

regions.name: Neighbour pointer E ($E6/$E7)
regions.description: Unless the column is 23 ($17): seek on to (row, column + 1); $E7 := 0 when there is none.

regions.name: Neighbour pointer S ($E8/$E9)
regions.description: Unless the row is 23: seek on to (row + 1, column); $E9 := 0 when there is none. RUN: a corner cell (0, 0) gave N = none, W = none, own = $8A6E, E = $8A71, S = $8ABC.

regions.name: SEEK: walk the world map to (row $18, column $19)
regions.description: Continues from the state in $14 (row) / $15 (column) / $17:$16 (record pointer) and stops when ($14, $15) equals ($18, $19). Each step adds the record's length, (first byte AND $0F) + 1, to the pointer; the column counter wraps at 24 and bumps the row. It only goes FORWARD, which is why the neighbours are fetched in raster order. See the world-map notes (24 x 24 records from $8A6E).

regions.name: READ THE RECORD (slot $8015): the room kind and the sub-id
regions.description: $5D := byte 0 AND $60 (the room kind: 0 plain, $20 item, $40 miniboss, $60 loop gate). Kinds $20 and $40 carry a sub-id: $5E := byte 3 and the field index $10 moves on to 4 ($10 starts at 3). Kinds 0 and $60 leave $5E UNCHANGED (stale from the last room). RUN. Sampled every kind: records [163 39 3 20] -> kind $20, sub-id 20; [67 102 25 30] -> $40, 30; kinds 0 and $60 left $5E alone.

regions.name: Read the record: the spawn-script id
regions.description: Byte 1 bit 3 = the room has enemies: then $57 := the next optional byte ($10 indexes it), with 0 read as 1; without the bit $57 := 0. RUN: [3 94 9 40] -> script 40; [2 54 9] -> 0.

regions.name: Read the record: the item type
regions.description: $55 := $A377[$5E]: the item a sub-id names (meaningful only for item rooms; for the others $5E is stale or a miniboss/other id and the value is unused). RUN: sub-id 20 -> $0E, 8 -> $0B.

regions.name: BUILD THE ROOM BUFFER (slot $8003): wait for the decompressor
regions.description: Slot $8003 -> $8155, called by every room loader ($EBC0, $EE80, $EEFD and others). JSR $C045 (-> $D7C3) waits until the tile decompressor is idle: the scene's tiles must be in before a room is drawn. (A harness without NMIs spins here; the checks below start at $8158.) The result is the 16 x 12 buffer at $0740 (192 bytes, one metatile id per 16-pixel cell, row by row) plus the four exit/key bytes $58-$5B and $54.

regions.name: Room buffer: pick the structure, door set and item list
regions.description: JSR $A749 selects the room's STRUCTURE ($18/$19), DOOR SET ($14/$15) and ITEM LIST ($16/$17): for an ordinary room entry 2 x $50 (the area) of the three tables, for a special screen the tables indexed by the screen type $51 (see the room-drawing notes).

regions.name: Room buffer: tile the structure's pattern
regions.description: A structure is [list offset][dest][width][height][pattern: width x height ids]. The pattern is copied into the buffer from offset dest and TILED: each row of the pattern repeats across to the end of the 16-cell row, rows are taken in turn, and after `height` rows the pattern starts again, until the buffer is full ($C0). A 1 x 1 structure is a plain floor. $12 is the row's start offset, $1B/$11 the width counter and width, $1A the rows left, $10 the pattern offset. RUN: the real routine built the room buffer for 302 rooms (ordinary rooms and special screens: every map record except the 21 gates and the empty cells) and the buffer equalled the independent model in tools/parse-structs.py in all of them, apart from the key-door cells noted at $82DD.

regions.name: Room buffer: the structure's own items
regions.description: The structure's first byte is an offset to a group of four [length][item] records (or to a zero byte for none); when it is not zero JSR $8379 draws them.

regions.name: Room buffer: the door set's four fixed items
regions.description: $19:$18 := the door set; $8379 draws its first four [length][item]s (walls and decoration that every room of the area has); $14 := the offset reached, where the four per-exit items follow.

regions.name: Room buffer: special screens have no exits
regions.description: $30 bit 5 (a special screen) skips the four exit walls and goes straight to the item list at $8227.

regions.name: Room buffer: read the openings
regions.description: $15 := byte 1 of the room's map record: bits 7, 6, 5, 4 = exits open to the north, west, east, south.

regions.name: Room buffer: north wall
regions.description: The door set's next item is the WALL across the north exit. It is drawn ($A6EB) when the north neighbour's record has bit 7 set in byte 0 (empty cell or special screen) or the room's north opening bit is clear; either way $14 advances past the item. So a wall is drawn across every exit that does not lead to an ordinary room.

regions.name: Room buffer: west wall
regions.description: The same with the west neighbour ($E2) and opening bit 6.

regions.name: Room buffer: east wall
regions.description: The same with the east neighbour ($E6) and opening bit 5.

regions.name: Room buffer: south wall
regions.description: The same with the south neighbour ($E8) and opening bit 4; an open south exit to an ordinary room jumps straight to $8227. At the map's EDGE the neighbour pointer has a high byte of 0 and the code reads ZERO PAGE: 47 rooms; the byte can have bit 7 set (129 and 137 were read), but the outcome is the same either way because an edge room has no opening there (all 47 matched the model).

regions.name: Room buffer: the item list
regions.description: The item list is a $0000-ended run of pointers to bare items [dest][width][height][tiles]; each is drawn with $A6EB (width bit 7 = one tile repeated, height bit 7 = the tiles are behind a pointer, $00 transparent). This is where a room's rocks, doors and decorations come from.

regions.name: Room buffer: the room's own layout pointer
regions.description: Byte 0 bit 4 of the record says a layout pointer is present, else jump to $82DD. The pointer follows the optional fields: Y = 3, +1 if there is a script id ($57), +1 if the kind is not 0 or $60 (a sub-id); $18/$19 := the layout.

regions.name: Layout: the shape and its fill tile
regions.description: A layout is [shape | count << 5][tile] + count x [tile][pos][mask | dir]. $8042 turns the shape number (byte 0 AND $1F) into the shape's address ($16); $10 := the tile; X := $20 (row 2 of the buffer).

regions.name: Layout: paint the shape
regions.description: The shape is 18 bytes of 1 bit per cell, most significant bit first: every set bit stores the tile at the next buffer cell (144 cells = rows 2-10).

regions.name: Layout: how many extra lines?
regions.description: Byte 0 bits 5-7 (rotated down) = the number of extra tile lines; zero goes to $82DD.

regions.name: Layout: paint the extra lines
regions.description: Each line is [tile][start position][mask | dir]: the top two bits of the third byte pick a step from the table at $82D9 (-15, +1, +16, +17: up-right, right, down, down-right) and the low six bits say which of the six cells along that direction receive the tile. Used for the lone rocks, doors and special tiles.

regions.name: Layout step directions: -15, 1, 16, 17
regions.description: $82B9 LDA $82D9,Y with Y = the top two bits of a layout item: the step $82A3 adds between the six cells of its mask in the 16-wide room buffer - up-right, right, down, down-right. The BNE / BEQ pair at $82D5 jumps over it.

regions.name: Key doors: reset the four exit keys
regions.description: $58-$5B := 8 for N, W, E, S: 'no key needed'.

regions.name: Key doors: the openings and this room's byte 0
regions.description: $15 and $54 := byte 1 of the record (the openings, bits 7-4, and bit 3 = the room has enemies: CORRECTION to the note that bit 3 of $54 was unexplained) and $14 := byte 0.

regions.name: Key doors: north exit
regions.description: If the north opening bit is set and (the neighbour's byte 0 OR this room's byte 0) has bit 7 set, a special screen lies on one side: the exit gets a KEY DOOR. $58 := the neighbour's byte 1 AND 7 (the key number its record names, 0 = no key) and metatile 8 (the door) is written to buffer cell $0777 (row 3, column 7). RUN: every exit whose $58-$5B was not 8 had metatile 8 in its door cell, and those were the only cells that differed from the model: 131 doors in the 302 rooms (1 door in 83 rooms, 2 in 19, 3 in 2, 4 in 1).

regions.name: Key doors: west exit
regions.description: The same for the west exit with opening bit 6: $59 and the door cell $07B2 (row 7, column 2). CORRECTION: the $0777 / $07B2 / $07BD / $07E7 lead in the weapons notes - they are these four door cells.

regions.name: Key doors: east exit
regions.description: $5A and the door cell $07BD (row 7, column 13).

regions.name: Key doors: south exit
regions.description: $5B and the door cell $07E7 (row 10, column 7); RTS. These four cells are the ones the cleared-gate code ($EEB7) opens (8 -> $0C).

regions.name: CELL CLASSES (slot $8006): the room buffer to the class map
regions.description: Called after a room is drawn (the scroll code ends with JMP $8006, and the loaders). Reads the 192 buffer cells $0740-$07FF two at a time, turns each metatile id into a class 0-14 through $838E, and packs the pair into one byte of $0400-$045F: the EVEN column in the HIGH nibble, the odd in the low (96 bytes). This map is what weapons, the ship and the item boxes look up. RUN over 312 ordinary rooms: equal to an independent model (class table below) in every room.

regions.name: Draw a group of four items
regions.description: Called from the room builder with Y = the offset of a run of [length][item] records at ($18): draws four of them with $A6EB (a counter of 4 on the stack; each step adds the record's length byte to Y). Y is returned past the fourth, so the caller can carry on (the door set's per-exit walls follow).

regions.name: Metatile id to cell class
regions.description: In: A = a room-buffer byte (set number in bits 5-7, metatile in bits 0-4); Y preserved. Sets 5-7 (A >= $A0): class 9. Sets 1-4 ($20-$9F): class 0. Set 0 ($00-$1F): the byte at $83A5 + id. RUN over all 256 values: exactly that. The class meanings (blocks, key-door cover, floor, sphere) are in the cells notes.

regions.name: Cell class by set-0 metatile id (ids 0-13)
regions.description: 00 08 07 06 05 01 04 04 0A 09 00 02 0E 00: ids 1 -> class 8, 2 -> 7, 3 -> 6, 4 -> 5, 5 -> 1, 6 -> 4, 7 -> 4, 8 -> 10, 9 -> 9, 10 -> 0, 11 -> 2, 12 -> 14, 13 -> 0. Only 14 entries: an id of 14-31 would read the CODE after the table (RUN: those give $A2, $0F, $86 ...), but no room buffer of the 312 ordinary rooms contains one (ids in sets 1-4 reach $89).

regions.name: DRAW 16 METATILES (slot $8009): find each metatile's five bytes
regions.description: Slot $8009. The 16 metatile ids of one 16-pixel band are in $04C0-$04CF (one band = 16 cells; $AE = the band index, whose parity picks the attribute half). For cell X = 15 down to 0 ($14): id bits 0-4 x 5 + the set's pointer ($0460,set lo / $0468,set hi) = the metatile's 5 bytes; id bits 5-7 = the set 0-7; $10 := the set's tile base ($0470,set). Called by the room-band drawer ($F03D), the corridor row builder ($E974) and the room-scroll code.

regions.name: Draw 16 metatiles: the four tiles
regions.description: The first four bytes of a metatile are its tiles top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right: each is $FF (blank: becomes tile $20) or the byte plus the set's tile base. They go to the band's two tile rows: $0130 + 2 x cell (top row, left and right) and $0150 + 2 x cell (bottom row). The 32-byte rows at $0130 and $0150 are what the NMI (or $E619) copies to the nametable.

regions.name: Draw 16 metatiles: the attribute quadrant
regions.description: The fifth byte: its low three bits pick an attribute pattern in $0199 (00 55 AA FF: the palette repeated in all four quadrants). The attribute byte of the 32 x 32 block ($04E8 + cell / 2; eight per band) is updated for this cell's QUADRANT only: index = column parity + 2 x band parity (top-left, top-right, bottom-left, bottom-right = bits 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6-7), the old two bits cleared with the mask $8469[index] and the pattern's two bits ORed in through $846D[index]. Two bands therefore build one attribute row; the second (odd) band completes it. RUN: all six attribute rows ($04E8, 48 bytes) of the labyrinth savestate's room were reproduced exactly.

regions.name: Draw 16 metatiles: write the fifth byte back, next cell
regions.description: $04C0 + cell := (the fifth byte AND $F0) OR the set number: the id byte is REPLACED by the object nibble (high 4 bits) and the set (low bits), which the ground-object spawner ($89FB, slot $802A) reads next. Then the next cell, until all 16 are done; RTS. RUN: the 768 tiles of the savestate room's 12 bands matched its nametable except 4 under an object (the one object-covered cell); written-back values 3 and 6 are the room's sets.

regions.name: Attribute clear masks by quadrant
regions.description: FC F3 CF 3F: clear bits 0-1, 2-3, 4-5, 6-7 of an attribute byte.

regions.name: Attribute quadrant masks by quadrant
regions.description: 03 0C 30 C0: the bits of the quadrant, ANDed with the pattern byte before it is ORed in.

regions.name: Dialogue: select a message (slot `$800C`)
regions.description: X = an object slot whose `$0620,X` holds the message number 0-20: `$05C0,X/$05D8,X` := the 16-bit pointer `$960F + 2 x number` (the pointer table in front of the dialogue script). Called when a type-`$34` message object is created. RUN: all 21 pointers equal the table.

regions.name: Dialogue: fetch the next two characters (slot `$800F`)
regions.description: Adds `$0638,X` (the bytes consumed last time) to the object's message pointer, stores it back, and reads two bytes: `$15` := the current character, `$14` := the one after it (a look-ahead), then `$0638,X` := 1. So each call advances one character. The script's controls are `$00` end of message, `$01` end of screenful, `$0D` end of line. RUN: for every message the first six calls returned (byte k, byte k+1) of the script.

regions.name: Clear the status screen's nametable, part 1: its attributes
regions.description: `JSR $C06C` (`$D5CC`) with four inline bytes `40 27 C0 00`: 64 bytes of `00` at PPU `$27C0`, the whole attribute table of nametable 1 (physical `$2400`: the status screen is drawn there, and so is the HUD). The call returns past the inline bytes, so execution carries on at `$84B0`. Called by the open (`$84DA`) and the close (`$8738`). RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate. After the close all 64 attribute bytes of nametable 1 are zero.

regions.name: Inline argument at $84AC
regions.description: 4 bytes of inline argument data following `JSR $D5CC` at bank 5 $84A9 - four-byte inline argument. The callee pops its own return address and reads these bytes through it, so they are data that happens to sit in the instruction stream, and a trace that decodes them produces nonsense that still looks like code. The length is not a guess: it is the constant the callee advances its own pointer by. What the bytes MEAN is not claimed. See annotations/dispatch.json for the routine and for how the class of these routines was enumerated.

regions.name: Clear the status screen's nametable, part 2: the rows
regions.description: `$14` := `$20` (the blank tile), `$15` := `$24` (nametable 1), `$17` := `$1C`, `$16` := `$18`, then `JMP $C084` (`$E453`, which clears rows `$17` up to `$16`-1 and wraps past row 29 to row 0): **rows 28, 29 and 0-23** of nametable 1. Rows 24-27 are left alone: that is where the HUD lives (25 SC/CHIP/SHOT, 26 the life meter, 27 AREA/X/Y). `$E453` returns to the caller of `$84A9`. RUN: after the close, rows 0-23, 28 and 29 of nametable 1 are all `$20`. RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate.

regions.name: Palette list: the status screen, 7 palettes and a skip
regions.description: A palette list for the walker at bank 7 $D92D (entered at $C05D with the pointer in $18/$19): for list position Y = 0-7 and a value below $FE it far-calls bank 5 $B2E4, which copies palette number A (three colours from the 36 x 3 table at bank 5 $B30A) to $0181 + 3Y; $FE ends the list, $FF skips the position. Positions 0-3 are the four background palettes and 4-7 the four sprite palettes. Read at bank 5 $84EE, in the status screen's open routine ($84CB): LDA #$C3 / STA $18 / LDA #$84 / STA $19 / JSR $C05D. The list is 05 0F 1F FF 00 01 02 03: background palettes 5, 15 and 31, position 3 skipped (the HUD-colour slot keeps what it had), and sprite palettes 0-3. Read from the code only; there is no status-screen savestate to compare with.

regions.name: Open: interrupts off, rendering off, save the palette
regions.description: STATUS SCREEN, OPEN (slot `$801B`, called from `$E500`): `SEI` (the DMC-timer IRQ that makes the HUD split is held off; this routine never clears the I flag, the close does), `JSR $C00F` (`$D4C1`: NMI off in `$FF`, rendering off in `$FE`), then the 24 palette bytes `$0181-$0198` are copied to `$04D0-$04E7` (the fade-target buffer, borrowed as a save area; `$0180`, the backdrop, is not saved). The close copies them back. RUN: after open + close the palette RAM equals the one before. RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate.

regions.name: Open: clear the screen, save sprite 0, hide the sprites
regions.description: `JSR $84A9` clears nametable 1. `$0177` := the Y of sprite 0 (`$0200`, the HUD split's marker, `$BF` in play), which the close puts back. `JSR $C015` (`$D534`) sets all 256 bytes of OAM to `$F8`: every sprite off screen, so the status screen starts with none (the entrance markers and the player's marker are added at the end of the open).

regions.name: Open: scroll and nametable
regions.description: `$FC` (the vertical scroll shadow) := `$B4` = 180 and `$A2` (the nametable select the NMI writes) := 1. Line 180 of the 240-line nametable is in row 22, so the screen's first visible rows are the bottom rows 28-29 of nametable 1 and then, wrapping, rows 0 on down: that is why the screen is built from rows 28, 29, 0-23 and why the 'KEY' row (29) sits above the key icons (rows 0-1). There is no raster split here (sprite 0 is hidden).

regions.name: Open: the palettes
regions.description: `$19:$18` := `$84C3` and `JSR $C05D` (`$D92D`, the palette-list walker): background palettes 0-2 := palettes 5, `$0F`, `$1F` of the 36 at `$B30A`, background palette 3 skipped (`$FF`, it keeps the play palette), sprite palettes 0-3 := palettes 0-3. Table at `$84C3`.

regions.name: Open: the marker colours, and upload both palettes
regions.description: `$0196` := `$16` and `$0197` := `$30`: the first two colours of sprite palette 3 (`$0196-$0198`) become red and white (the third, `$0198`, stays `$0F`), the colours of the map's entrance and player markers. `$017F` := 3: upload both background and sprite palettes (bits 0 and 1; see the palette-upload entry in the RAM map). RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate. Palette RAM after the open ends `... 16 30 0F`.

regions.name: Open: load the map's quadrant tiles
regions.description: `$19:$18` := `$1010`, A := 3, Y := 2, `JSR $C042` (`$D7F9`): arm the decompressor with **block 3 of bank 2** (the block at bank 2 `$959F`, 240 bytes = 15 tiles) for PPU `$1010-$10FF`: background tiles `$01-$0F`. Tile k is the map's quadrant tile: each of its four 4x4-pixel quadrants is filled when the matching bit of k is set (1 top left, 2 top right, 4 bottom left, 8 bottom right), colours 1 and 2, tile 15 solid. The map drawer `$891F` picks the tile by OR-ing those bits. RUN: all 15 tiles decoded from the ROM equal the live CHR after the open, and each tile's four quadrant fills equal its bits. RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate.

regions.name: Open: the frame tile (tile $00)
regions.description: `JSR $C06F` with a 19-byte inline PPU string `10 10 00` + 16 bytes: tile `$00` of pattern table 1 (PPU `$1000`) := plane 0 all `00`, plane 1 `FF 80 80 80 80 80 80 80`: colour 2 along the top row and the left column. It is the map frame's line tile (and is also the first key-door picture's tile `$00`: the close rebuilds that).

regions.name: Queued PPU write at $8518
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $8515. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $1000 is in the block itself. The block is 19 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. The 16 payload bytes are '................' read as ASCII, which is not text - so they are tile numbers for something drawn rather than written, and this region is kind data on that ground alone. Characters are ASCII for the letters and space. NOT ESTABLISHED: the glyphs for codes outside A-Z and space, which only the font can settle - and no font has been found yet, because CHR is RAM on this cartridge.

regions.name: Open: the word KEY
regions.description: `JSR $C06F`, inline `03 27 B0` + 'KEY': the label at PPU `$27B0`, row 29 column 16 of nametable 1 (the top row of the screen, over the key icons).

regions.name: "KEY" at $852E
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $852B. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $27B0 is in the block itself. The block is 6 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. It reads "KEY". Characters are ASCII for the letters and space. NOT ESTABLISHED: the glyphs for codes outside A-Z and space, which only the font can settle - and no font has been found yet, because CHR is RAM on this cartridge.

regions.name: Open: draw the map, then start the weapon icon upload loop
regions.description: `JSR $8805` first: the world map (the frame table `$87E4`, then the map itself; the next stretch). Then Y := 0 and `$19:$18` := `$1800`: the loop that uploads the 12 weapon icons.

regions.name: Open: upload one weapon icon
regions.description: Save `$18`, `$19` and Y on the stack, then a far call (inline `02 02 80`) to bank 2 `$8003` (-> `$81B2`, the icon uploader) with A = Y: icon Y of the 18 at bank 2 `$8E0C` (four 2-bpp tiles, 64 bytes) goes to PPU `$19:$18`. RUN: the 12 icons 0-11 at `$1800 + 64 k` equal bank 2 `$8E0C + 64 k` in the live CHR after the open.

regions.name: Far-call argument at $854A
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $8547 - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 2 $8003**. The stored word is $8002 rather than $8003 because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Open: weapon icon loop
regions.description: Restore Y and the pointer, add `$40` to it (the next icon's 64 bytes), Y++; repeat until Y = 12: PPU `$1800-$1AFF` holds the 12 weapon icons.

regions.name: Open: start the key icon loop
regions.description: Y := 1 and the same save/far-call shape, now to bank 2 `$8006` (-> `$8212`, the key-icon builder, inline `02 05 80`) with A = Y = the key number 1-7: PPU `$1B00 + 64 (k-1)`, so `$1B00-$1CBF` hold the seven key pictures (the pointer carries on from `$1B00`, where the weapon loop left it).

regions.name: Far-call argument at $856E
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $856B - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 2 $8006**. The stored word is $8005 rather than $8006 because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Open: key icon loop
regions.description: Restore, pointer += `$40`, Y++, loop until Y = 8 (seven keys).

regions.name: Open: the level pips
regions.description: A far call (inline `00 17 80`) to bank 0 `$8018` (-> `$8034`): a `JSR $C06F` with 35 inline bytes that write 32 bytes at PPU `$1CC0`: **tiles `$CC` and `$CD`**, the two small pictures that the ATTACK and SHIELD rows repeat once per level (`$CD` for attack, `$CC` for shield). RUN: `$1CC0-$1CDF` equal those 32 bytes after the open.

regions.name: Far-call argument at $8588
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $8585 - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 0 $8018**. The stored word is $8017 rather than $8018 because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Open: the slot loop (20 slots)
regions.description: `$16` walks the 20 slots of the table `$8690` in steps of 4 (Y = `$16`): slots 0-6 are the keys, slot 7 (Y = `$1C`) is the zero slot and is skipped, slots 8-19 are the 12 weapons. Each slot: the cell to draw at `[ppu lo][ppu hi]`, its attribute address and its tile.

regions.name: Open: a key slot - owned or not
regions.description: Y below `$1C`: n := Y/4 (key n+1), `JSR $C078` (`$EFC7`, bit n -> mask), AND `$04B0` (the keys held): A := 1 if the key is held, else 0; pushed. (The weapon branch is the `BCS` at `$8596`.) RUN: with `$04B0` = `$55` keys 1, 3, 5, 7 were drawn and 2, 4, 6 blank.

regions.name: Open: a weapon slot - its level
regions.description: Y above `$1C`: weapon number := Y/4 - 8 (0-11; the `LSR`s leave carry clear, so the `SBC #$07` subtracts 8), `JSR $C075` (`$E498`: the 2-bit level of that weapon from `$04AC-$04AE`, 0-3, 0 = not owned); pushed. The first `$18`/`$19` stored here (the slot address with the row ORed with `$20`) are overwritten at `$85C7`: dead stores.

regions.name: Open: draw the slot's picture
regions.description: A (the key flag, or the weapon level) indexes `$85DA`: `$17` := `00 00 55 AA` = the attribute pattern mask (keys always 0; weapons level 0-1 palette 0, level 2 palette 1, level 3 palette 2). `$18`/`$19` := the slot's PPU address. The pushed value is pulled: zero (key not held, weapon not owned) draws tile `$20`, the blank; otherwise the slot's own tile (`$8693,Y`).

regions.name: Icon attribute by weapon level: 00 00 55 AA
regions.description: Read by $85C2 LDA $85DA,Y with Y = 0 or 1 for a key (held or not) and 0-3 for a weapon (its level from $C075), giving the attribute byte that picks the icon's palette: level 2 gets palette 1, level 3 palette 2. CORRECTION: the trace decoded $85DA as a BRK. It is never executed - the instruction before it is LDA #$20 / BNE, which always branches.

regions.name: Open: draw one 16x16 cell and step to the next slot
regions.description: Tile in A, the slot's attribute address (`$8692,Y`) in Y, `JSR $C054` (`$D865`): queue a 2x2 cell at PPU `$19:$18` with that tile as base, the attribute byte at the given address updated with the pattern mask `$17`. The four tiles go in the order base, base+2 (top row) and base+1, base+3 (bottom). Then `$16` += 4; at `$50` (20 slots) the loop ends, else `JMP $858D`. RUN: with weapon levels `$04AC` = `E4`, `$04AD` = `1B`, `$04AE` = `C1` the owned weapons showed their slot tile and the others blank. RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate.

regions.name: Open: 'NO' for the weapon window
regions.description: `JSR $C06F`, inline `02 2D C2` + 'NO': PPU `$2DC2` (row 14, column 2). With the next string, 'USE' at row 15, it is the default text of the A-button weapon window; what the per-frame handler `$8937` does with it when a weapon is selected is the next stretch.

regions.name: "NO" at $85FA
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $85F7. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $2DC2 is in the block itself. The block is 5 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. It reads "NO". Characters are ASCII for the letters and space. NOT ESTABLISHED: the glyphs for codes outside A-Z and space, which only the font can settle - and no font has been found yet, because CHR is RAM on this cartridge.

regions.name: Open: 'USE'
regions.description: `JSR $C06F`, inline `03 2D E2` + 'USE': PPU `$2DE2` (row 15, column 2).

regions.name: "USE" at $8602
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $85FF. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $2DE2 is in the block itself. regions.name: Open: the weapon's power and chips per use
regions.description: `JSR $89CB`: prints the selected weapon's level `$3D` (one ASCII digit, PPU `$2D3D`) and the chips per use `$45` (three digits at `$2D5B`), the numbers beside WEAPON POWER and USE CHIP. **CORRECTION: an earlier version of this note called `$89CB` 'the map's markers'; the entrance markers are drawn by `$8805`'s own loop.** It is also called by the per-frame handler (`$89BF`).

regions.name: Open: sprite tables, and remember the weapon
regions.description: `$FF` := (`$FF` AND `$DF`) OR `$08`, written to PPUCTRL: 8x8 sprites (bit 5 clear) from pattern table 1 (bit 3), the table whose tile `$01` is the map's marker. `$0176` := `$3C`, the selected weapon, for the close to compare. RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate. PPUCTRL `$B1` became `$99`.

regions.name: Open: start the cursor repeat counter, blink the marker
regions.description: `$15` := 5 and `$14` := 0, then a far call (inline `02 1D 80`) to bank 2 `$801E` (-> `$8998`), the blinking player marker (it writes the last four sprites, OAM `$02F0-$02FF`, one pattern per call; it reads neither `$14` nor `$15`). **CORRECTION: the 5 and 0 are not arguments of `$8998` (the first version of this note called them a lead): `$15` is the cursor handler's auto-repeat counter, read only by `$8946`, so a direction held from before the screen opened waits 5 frames; `$14` is not read by the handler.** The marker sits at (column x 4 + `$10`, row x 4 + `$3B`) = (`$30`, `$6B`) for position (8, 12).

regions.name: Far-call argument at $868A
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $8687 - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 2 $801E**. The stored word is $801D rather than $801E because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Open: picture on
regions.description: `JMP $C063` (`$EDF4`): wait for the vertical blank, NMI on, two frames, rendering on (`$D4D5`). It does not execute the `CLI` of `$EDF2`: after the open the I flag is still set (RUN: P = `$24`).

regions.name: Status screen slot layout: 20 x [ppu lo][ppu hi][attr lo][tile]
regions.description: Twenty 4-byte records, walked by $858B with Y stepping by 4 to CPY #$50. Slots 0-6 are the seven keys, on nametable row 0 from column 16 in steps of 2, tiles $B0-$C8; slot 7 is all zero and skipped by CPY #$1C; slots 8-19 are the twelve weapons in a grid at rows 14, 16 and 18, tiles $80-$AC. CHECKS: the tile numbers are exactly where the uploaders put the art ($1800 = tile $80, $1B00 = tile $B0), and every third byte is the correct attribute-table address for its slot's position, e.g. row 14 column 8 -> $DA.

regions.name: HUD SHOT icon: blank
regions.description: `JSR $C06F` with a 9-byte attribute-cell item `C7 3C 20 20 20 20 F7 00 FF`: the 2x2 cell at PPU `$273C` (nametable 1 row 25, column 28, right of the word SHOT) gets four blank tiles `$20`, attribute address `$F7` (`$27F7`), mask `00`, pattern `FF`. The item layout is the one `$D865` writes: `[C0 | hi][lo][t0][t1][t2][t3][attr address lo][mask][pattern]`.

regions.name: Queued PPU write at $86E3
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $86E0. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $3C20 is in the block itself. The block is 9 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. The 6 payload bytes are '   ...' read as ASCII, which is not text - so they are tile numbers for something drawn rather than written, and this region is kind data on that ground alone. The count byte is $C7, at or above $C0, so its length is the fixed 9 rather than a character count - the one branch of $D591 that does not derive the length from the byte. Characters are ASCII for the letters and space. NOT ESTABLISHED: the glyphs for codes outside A-Z and space, which only the font can settle - and no font has been found yet, because CHR is RAM on this cartridge.

regions.name: HUD SHOT icon: return
regions.description: RTS of the blank case.

regions.name: REFRESH THE SHOT ICON IN THE HUD (slot `$8033`)
regions.description: Called by the close (`$8715`), by `$89BC` in the per-frame handler and, through the slot, by the weapon cursor code in other banks. `$3C` zero: `BEQ $86E0` draws the blank cell. Otherwise `JSR $C06F` with the item `C7 3C 3C 3E 3D 3F F7 00 FF`: PPU `$273C`, tiles `$3C $3E` over `$3D $3F`, the four tiles that `$86FD` uploads the weapon's icon to. RUN: weapon 3 -> after the NMI drained the queue, nametable 1 rows 25-26 columns 28-29 read `3C 3E / 3D 3F`; weapon 0 -> `20 20 / 20 20`.

regions.name: Queued PPU write at $86F4
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $86F1. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $3C3C is in the block itself. The block is 9 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. regions.name: SHOT icon: upload the weapon's picture
regions.description: `$19:$18` := `$13C0` (tiles `$3C-$3F` of table 1) and A := `$3C` - 1, a far call (inline `02 02 80`) to bank 2 `$8003` (the icon uploader): icon (weapon - 1) of the 18 at bank 2 `$8E0C` becomes the HUD's weapon picture. (The queue item has been written first; the NMI drains both.) Not verified byte for byte: the harness's NMI had not drained the upload when read.

regions.name: Far-call argument at $870D
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $870A - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 2 $8003**. The stored word is $8002 rather than $8003 because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: SHOT icon: return
regions.description: RTS.

regions.name: STATUS SCREEN, CLOSE (slot `$801E`, called from `$E50F`): off, and refresh the SHOT icon
regions.description: STATUS SCREEN, CLOSE (slot `$801E`, called from `$E50F`): `SEI`, `JSR $C00F` (NMI and rendering off), `JSR $86ED` (the HUD's weapon icon for the weapon as it is now). RUN: bank 5 live, `$84CB` then `$8711` called on the labyrinth savestate.

regions.name: Close: a different weapon was chosen
regions.description: `$3C` compared with `$0176` (the weapon on entry). **Different:** `JSR $C048` (`$CCBF`, remove an object) for slots 3 and 4, the A-button weapon's objects, and unless `$30` bit 3 is set (the launch/landing flight) `JSR $C069` (`$F726`, load the sprite tiles of the selected weapon). Same: skipped. RUN: weapon 3 -> 5: `$CCBF` called for slots 3 and 4, `$F726` called, and the sprite tiles changed; 3 -> 3: neither called.

regions.name: Close: HUD uses-left, sprites off, clear the screen
regions.description: `JSR $C072` (`$E1C3`) reprints `$3E`, the uses left, in the HUD; `JSR $C015` hides all sprites; `JSR $84A9` clears nametable 1.

regions.name: Close: sprite tables back
regions.description: `$FF` := (`$FF` AND `$F7`) OR `$20` to PPUCTRL: 8x16 sprites, sprite table 0 again.

regions.name: Close: reload the scene
regions.description: `LDA $5C / JSR $ACA9`: load the current scene again (tile blocks to the background CHR, metatile sets, palettes) - this overwrites the status screen's CHR at `$1000-$1CDF`. **`$30` bit 6 set (a corridor):** also scene 1, the corridors' common scene, then `JMP $8760`. Clear (the labyrinth): carry on at `$8757`. RUN: corridor close called `$ACA9` with `$5C` then 1 and did not call `$ED51`.

regions.name: Close, labyrinth: key-door pictures
regions.description: `JSR $C08A` (`$ED51`): rebuild the key pictures for this room's exits in background tiles `$00-$07` (see the key-door entry). RUN: with exits (3, 8, 8, 5) tiles `$00-$03` equal the key-3 icon built on its own after the close, `$04-$07` hold key 5's; with no key doors tile `$00` keeps the frame tile (harmless: no key door is drawn).

regions.name: Close, labyrinth: the eight glyphs
regions.description: A far call (inline `02 0B 80`) to bank 2 `$800C` (-> `$8153`): the font record set 1, eight glyphs into background tiles `$08-$0F` (PPU `$1080-$10FF`), which the map's quadrant tiles had replaced. Together with `$ED51` this restores tiles `$00-$0F`. RUN: after the close CHR `$1080-$10FF` equals its value before the open.

regions.name: Far-call argument at $875D
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $875A - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 2 $800C**. The stored word is $800B rather than $800C because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Close: restore the palette
regions.description: `$04D0-$04E7` are copied back to `$0181-$0198` (the copy the open made).

regions.name: Close: upload the palette, wait for the tiles, commit the scroll
regions.description: `$017F` := 3 (both palettes), `JSR $C045` (`$D7C3`: wait for the decompressor), `JSR $C087` (`$E522`: write the scroll variables back to the shadow registers, which restores `$FC` and the nametable select from `$A6`-`$A9`). RUN: after the close `$FC` = 0, `$A2` = 0 as before.

regions.name: Close: one object-loop pass
regions.description: A far call (inline `06 FF 7F`) to bank 6 `$8000`, the object loop: every object runs once and draws its sprites into the OAM the open emptied. That is the reading of why it is here; the caller `$E515` does one more pass after the close returns.

regions.name: Far-call argument at $8779
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $8776 - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 6 $8000**. The stored word is $7FFF rather than $8000 because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Close: sprite 0 back, picture on
regions.description: `LDA $0177 / JMP $C060` (`$EDE5`): `JSR $D51E` sets sprite 0's Y from A (the HUD split's marker), then the code falls into `$EDE8`: DMC rate `$87`, `$EDF4` (vblank sync, NMI on, two frames, rendering on), **`CLI`** - the interrupt flag the open set is cleared here (RUN: P `$24` after the open, `$21` after the close).

regions.name: ATTACK row: the label
regions.description: `JSR $C06F`, inline `06 2C B0` + 'ATTACK': PPU `$2CB0` (row 5, column 16).

regions.name: "ATTACK" at $8785
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $8782. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $2CB0 is in the block itself. The block is 9 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. It reads "ATTACK". Characters are ASCII for the letters and space. NOT ESTABLISHED: the glyphs for codes outside A-Z and space, which only the font can settle - and no font has been found yet, because CHR is RAM on this cartridge.

regions.name: ATTACK row: its pips
regions.description: `$19:$18` := `$2CB7`, `$15` := `$CD` (the pip tile) and A := `$4A`, the attack level, then `JMP $87B9`.

regions.name: SHIELD row: the label
regions.description: `JSR $C06F`, inline `06 2C D0` + 'SHIELD': PPU `$2CD0` (row 6, column 16).

regions.name: "SHIELD" at $87A2
regions.description: A queued PPU write item, written inline after `JSR $D576` at bank 5 $879F. Its shape is [count][ppu_hi][ppu_lo][count characters]: the destination $2CD0 is in the block itself. The block is 9 bytes and the caller resumes immediately after it; the length comes from the first byte by the rule in $D591 - (byte & $7F) + 3 below $C0, 9 at or above - and $D5A5 advances the routine's own pointer by exactly that. It reads "SHIELD". Characters are ASCII for the letters and space. NOT ESTABLISHED: the glyphs for codes outside A-Z and space, which only the font can settle - and no font has been found yet, because CHR is RAM on this cartridge.

regions.name: SHIELD row: its pips
regions.description: `$19:$18` := `$2CD7`, `$15` := `$CC` and A := `$4B`, the shield level; falls into `$87B9`.

regions.name: Level pips: nothing to draw
regions.description: A (the level) zero: RTS.

regions.name: Level pips: queue a run of A tiles
regions.description: `$C04B` (`$D6D3`) waits until the PPU queue has room for A + 3 bytes, `$C03C` (`$D6E0`) reserves the entry; the entry is `[A][hi $19][lo $18]` followed by A copies of the pip tile `$15`, and `JMP $C03F` (`$D6F7`) commits it. RUN: attack level 2 -> two `$CD` at row 5 columns 23-24; shield level 3 -> three `$CC` at row 6 columns 23-25.

regions.name: Status map frame: 8 runs + $FF
regions.description: Eight [count][ppu hi][ppu lo][tile] records and a $FF terminator, read by $8805 and each passed to C036 ($D5F8), which writes `tile` count AND $7F times - across, or down when bit 7 of the count is set. Two horizontal edges of 14, two vertical of 12 and four corners: the box around the 12 x 12-tile map.

regions.name: Map: wait for the pending row
regions.description: WORLD MAP ON THE STATUS SCREEN (`$8805`, called from the open): `LDA $A5 / BNE` spins until `$A5` (the one half-sent background row) is zero, so the frame and map go into an idle queue.

regions.name: Map: the frame
regions.description: X walks the table `$87E4` in fours (`$FF` ends): `$15` := count, `$19:$18` := PPU address, `$14` := tile, `JSR $C036` (`$D5F8`) queues a run of `count AND $7F` tiles (down when bit 7 is set): the box around the map (two horizontal edges, two vertical edges, four corners).

regions.name: Map: set up the walk
regions.description: `$1B:$1A` := `$8A6E` (the world map's first record), `$19:$18` := `$2C02` (nametable 1 row 0, column 2: the first of 12 map rows), `$17` := 0 (the OAM offset for the entrance markers), `$14` := 0 (the map row). The map is 24 x 24 records but is drawn 12 x 12 tiles: each tile covers a 2 x 2 block of records.

regions.name: Map: clear the tile-row buffer
regions.description: `$0150-$015B` (12 bytes) := 0: one nametable row of map tiles, each tile the OR of its four quadrant bits.

regions.name: Map: column := 0
regions.description: `$15` := 0, the map column. It is entered twice per tile row, once for each of the two map rows that make it, without clearing the buffer in between.

regions.name: Map: an empty record?
regions.description: Byte 0 of the record at `($1A)` equal to `$80` is an empty cell: skip to the advance at `$88B9`.

regions.name: Map: is the cell revealed?
regions.description: Byte 1 AND 7 is the key that reveals the cell: 0 = always shown; otherwise key k is tested as bit k-1 of `$04B0` through `$C078`; not held skips the cell. RUN: with `$04B0` = 0 only the key-0 cells appeared; with `$FF` all. RUN: the open `$84CB` on the labyrinth savestate with chosen keys and clear flags.

regions.name: Map: put the cell in the buffer
Map: an area entrance?
regions.description: Byte 0 bit 7 and byte 2 bit 7 must both be set (a special screen that is a corridor gate); either clear skips to the advance.

regions.name: Map: should the marker show?
regions.description: The corridor number is byte 2 AND `$7F`. **Corridor 21:** shown when `($04AA OR $FC) AND $04A9` = `$FF`, i.e. corridors 1-10 are all cleared - and it is **not** hidden again once corridor 21 itself is cleared. **Any other corridor:** `JSR $C07B` (`$EFAC`), shown only while its cleared flag is clear (carry set). RUN: with all flags `FF FF FF` exactly one marker (corridor 21's) remained; with none cleared, the 20 corridor markers appeared (keys `FF`). RUN: the open `$84CB` on the labyrinth savestate with chosen keys and clear flags.

regions.name: Map: write the entrance marker sprite
regions.description: A sprite at OAM offset `$17`: x = column x 4 + `$10`, y = row x 4 + `$3B`, tile 1, attribute 3 (sprite palette 3, red and white), then `$17` += 4. RUN: the sprites of ten random key/flag settings equalled an independent model of this rule in every case (0 to 20 markers).

regions.name: Map: next record
regions.description: `$1A:$1B` += (byte 0 AND `$0F`) + 1, the record length (the `SEC` before the `ADC` is the plus one).

regions.name: Map: next column
regions.description: `$15`++; at 24 the row is finished, else back to `$8853`.

regions.name: Map: next row
regions.description: `$14`++; an odd count means one more map row goes into the same tile row (back to `$884F`); an even count falls into the flush.

regions.name: Map: queue one row of 12 tiles
regions.description: Room for 15 bytes in the PPU queue (`$C04B`), entry `[$0C][$19][$18]` + the 12 buffer bytes (a zero becomes the blank `$20`), the address then += `$20` (next tile row). RUN: all 144 tiles (12 x 12) equalled the model's quadrant-bit tiles in the ten cases, zero showing as `$20`. RUN: the open `$84CB` on the labyrinth savestate with chosen keys and clear flags.

regions.name: Map: more rows?
regions.description: `$14` = 24 ends (RTS); else back to `$8845` for the next tile row.

regions.name: Map: add this cell's quadrant to its tile
regions.description: Bit value: row even 1 / row odd 4, doubled when the column is odd (so 1 top left, 2 top right, 4 bottom left, 8 bottom right); X := column / 2; `$0150,X` OR= the bit. The tile number is the OR, and bank 2 block 3 holds the tile for each of the 15 values (see the open).

regions.name: STATUS SCREEN, EVERY FRAME (slot `$8021`, called from `$E506`): any button?
regions.description: `$F5 OR $F6` is the pads' NEW presses (both ports), `$F7 OR $F8` the HELD buttons. A new press goes to `$8951`; nothing held ends at `$89C5`; held without a new press goes on to the repeat counter. The wait for Start/Select to leave is `$E509-$E50D` in the caller, not here.

regions.name: Cursor: auto-repeat
regions.description: `$15` is decremented; not yet zero ends at `$89C5`; zero reloads it with 6. A new press (`$8951`) loads 20 instead. RUN (hold Right from a new press): moves at calls 0, 20, 26, 32, 38, 44: one at once, the next after 20 calls, then every 6.

regions.name: Cursor: first-press delay
regions.description: A := 20, stored in `$15` at `$8953` (6 comes in here from `$894D`).

regions.name: Cursor: direction
regions.description: The held buttons' low four bits (Right 1, Left 2, Down 4, Up 8); none ends at `$89C5`. This is also where an unowned weapon sends control back to keep moving.

regions.name: Cursor: Right
regions.description: `$3C`++; 13 wraps to 0.

regions.name: Cursor: Left
regions.description: `$3C`--; below 0 becomes 12.

regions.name: Cursor: Up
regions.description: `$3C` - 5 if that is not negative, else `$3C` + 10, and if that is 13 or more, `$3C` + 5. The cursor positions are 0 (no weapon) and 1-12 in rows of five. RUN: all 13 positions x 4 directions with every weapon owned equalled this reading and its Down twin (Up: 0->10, 1->11, 2->12, 3->8, 5->0, 12->7).

regions.name: Cursor: Down
regions.description: `$3C` + 5 if under 13; 15 or more: minus 15 more; 13 or 14: minus 10 (carry clear), so Down from 8 is 3 and from 10 is 0.

regions.name: Cursor: store
regions.description: `STA $3C`.

regions.name: Cursor: sound, and the weapon's level
regions.description: Sound `$3E` (`$D852`), then `JSR $C135` (`$FD77`), which puts the weapon's level in `$3D` (the notes on weapons).

regions.name: Cursor: skip a weapon that is not owned
regions.description: `$3C` zero (no weapon) is always allowed; otherwise `$3D` zero (level 0, not owned) goes back to `$8955` and moves again in the held direction. RUN: with weapons 2, 5 and 12 owned, Right from 0 gave 2, 5, 12, 0, 2; Left from 0 gave 12.

regions.name: Cursor: refresh the HUD and the numbers
regions.description: `JSR $86ED` (the SHOT icon), `JSR $C072` (the uses left), `JSR $89CB` (power and chips per use).

regions.name: Every frame: the blinking marker
regions.description: Far call (inline `02 1D 80`) to bank 2 `$801E` (-> `$8998`), reached from every path of the handler. The return address skips the inline bytes and the code runs on into `$89CB`, so the numbers are also reprinted on every frame.

regions.name: Far-call argument at $89C8
regions.description: Three bytes of far-call argument following `JSR $D76F` at bank 5 $89C5 - bank number, then the target address minus one, little-endian. They select **bank 2 $801E**. The stored word is $801D rather than $801E because $D790 pushes these two bytes as a fake return address and lets RTS add the one back; that is not an inference, it is what the four instructions at $D799-$D7A4 do. A far call is the one reference in this ROM that no grep for an operand will ever surface, so the target is recorded here where a reader will find it.

regions.name: Print the weapon's power
regions.description: Room for 4 bytes, entry `[01][$2D][$3D][$3D + $30]`: the level `$3D` as an ASCII digit at PPU `$2D3D` (row 9, column 29), next to WEAPON POWER. RUN: `$3D` = 3 gave '3'.

regions.name: Print the chips per use
regions.description: `$19:$18` := `$2D5B` and A := `$45` (the chips one use costs, `$FDD3` table), `JMP $C051` (`$E1CD`): three blank-suppressed digits at row 10, columns 27-29. RUN: `$45` = 25 gave ' 25'.

regions.name: Ground objects: the row's y
regions.description: GROUND-OBJECT SPAWNER (slot `$802A`, called by the row drawers `$E974` and `$EFF3` after `$83B3` has drawn 16 metatiles): `$14` := (`$E8` + `$AF` - `$B7`) AND `$FF`: the y every object of this row gets (`$AF` is the scroll position within a 16-pixel row, `$B7` the scroll step). RUN: `$AF` = 5, `$B7` = 2 gave y `$EB`. RUN: synthetic row buffers on the labyrinth savestate (bank 5 live): cells with high nibbles 1-7, sets mapped to the three lists.

regions.name: Ground objects: start at cell 15
regions.description: X := 15; the 16 cells of `$04C0-$04CF` are taken from the last to the first (so cell 15 gets the highest free slot).

regions.name: Ground objects: does the cell name an object?
regions.description: `$04C0,X` AND `$F0`: `$83B3` wrote each cell's fifth metatile byte there as (high nibble, set) - the high nibble is the object number within the set's list. Zero: next cell.

regions.name: Ground objects: find the set's object list
regions.description: The low nibble of the cell is the metatile set (0-7); `$0478 + set` (loaded by the scene's set records, `[set | list << 4]`) is the list number 0-2; `$11:$12` := the pointer at `$803C + 2 x list`: `$AF61`, `$AF69`, `$AF71` (8 bytes each); Y := the high nibble.

regions.name: Ground objects: the type
regions.description: The list's byte at Y is the object type; zero means none (next cell); else `$15` := type. RUN: list 0 = `00 31 36 37 3C 75 76 7C`, list 1 = `7D 38 39 3A 3A 3B 3C 3D`, list 2 = `3F 7F 7E 7E 7A 05 03 00`; every spawned type equalled list[set's list][nibble]. RUN: synthetic row buffers on the labyrinth savestate (bank 5 live): cells with high nibbles 1-7, sets mapped to the three lists.

regions.name: Ground objects: a slot
regions.description: `JSR $C027` (`$EA8C`, the allocator: highest free slot 5-23, else reclaim). Carry set (none) ends the WHOLE routine at `$8A6D`, the remaining cells of the row are not tried. RUN: with all 19 slots holding an unreclaimable type nothing changed.

regions.name: Ground objects: type and cell byte
regions.description: Slot field 0 (`$0500,Y`) := the type; field 17 (`$0698,Y`) := the whole cell byte (nibble and set) - the field is the aiming speed class for moving objects and is simply reused here by the ground objects' handlers.

regions.name: Ground objects: band and tile address
regions.description: Field 10 (`$05F0`) := `$AE`, the row index; fields 8 and 9 (`$05C0`, `$05D8`) := the PPU address of the cell's top left tile, `$AD:$AC` + 2 x cell. The handlers use them to patch the background (the cannons' animation through `$AA21`).

regions.name: Ground objects: x
regions.description: Field 2 (`$0530`) := 16 x cell + 8, the cell's centre. RUN: cells 3, 4, 7, 9, 12, 15 gave x `$38 $48 $78 $98 $C8 $F8`.

regions.name: Ground objects: y and attribute address
regions.description: Field 1 (`$0518`) := `$14`; field 11 (`$0608`) := `$AA` + cell / 2, the low byte of the cell's attribute-table address (two cells per attribute byte).

regions.name: Ground objects: next cell
regions.description: DEX; loop while X >= 0.

regions.name: Ground objects: return
regions.description: RTS (also the exit when no slot is free).

regions.name: World map: 24 x 24 rooms
regions.description: 576 variable-length records, 24 rows of 24 - one per room of the labyrinth. A record is (first byte AND $0F) + 1 bytes ($8103: LDA ($16),Y / AND #$0F / SEC / ADC $16). $80F5 seeks through it; $8071 walks it as the player moves ($52 column, $53 row); $882D draws it on the status screen as 2x2-cell background tiles, sprites marking corridor entrances only. BYTE 0: low nibble length-1, $80 exactly empty, bit 4 = layout pointer present, bits 5-6 = room kind ($5D; $20 and $40 carry a sub-id). BYTE 1: low three bits = the KEY that reveals the cell ($04B0), bit 3 = the room has enemies, bits 7/6/5/4 = openings north/west/east/south ($82DD against the neighbours $E0/$E2/$E6/$E8), and byte 0 bit 7 puts a key door in an opening. BYTE 2: bit 7 = corridor entrance, low seven bits = corridor number. THEN, in order: sub-id ($5E), spawn script id ($57, into $A4C7), layout pointer. CHECKS: 370 of 370 non-empty records are exactly as long as their flags imply; corridor numbers 1-21 occur once each; in the labyrinth savestate the live room pointer $E4 = $8E4C is this walk's row 12 column 8, and that room's layout and openings match the nametable cell for cell; 211 rooms with enemies use script ids 1-47, 47 distinct. CORRECTION: this region was first 807 records running to $960E, proved by 'the walk lands exactly on $960F' - a weak test that a walk over arbitrary data passes about one time in four. The map ends at $91EA, which $8042 names as the room-shape base. Generated by tools/parse-map.py.

regions.name: Room shapes: 19 x 18 bytes, 1bpp
regions.description: 19 room shapes. $8042 computes $91EA + 18 * (A AND $1F), and $8278 shifts the 18 bytes out one bit at a time (CPY #$12) into the 16-wide room buffer at $0740 from index $20, writing the layout's fill tile wherever a bit is set: 144 cells, rows 2-10. THE EXTENT: the layouts use shapes 0-18, and 19 x 18 bytes from $91EA end exactly where the layout chain begins. Generated by tools/parse-map.py.

regions.name: Room layouts: 79
regions.description: 79 room layouts, read by $8243 through the pointer at the end of a map record. [shape | count << 5][fill tile], then count x [tile][position][six-bit mask | direction]: $82A3 walks the mask along a step from $82D9 (-15, 1, 16, 17 - up-right, right, down, down-right), writing the tile at each set bit. So a layout is 2 + 3 * count bytes. THE CHECK: chained from $9340 the layouts land exactly on $960F, and all 67 layouts the map points at are on the chain; 12 are not pointed at by any map record. Generated by tools/parse-map.py.

regions.name: Dialogue message pointer table
regions.description: 21 little-endian pointers, $960F-$9638, into the dialogue script that follows immediately. Read by bank 5 $8476: LDA $0620,X gives an object's message number, ASL A doubles it into Y, and LDA $960F,Y / LDA $9610,Y fetch the two halves - so the base in the operand is this region's own address, which is the strongest statement available that the table starts here. The entry count is bounded by structure, not by the reader: 21 x 2 = 42 bytes ends at $9639, exactly where the first message begins, with nothing over. NOTHING IN THE CODE BOUNDS IT - the index comes from $0620,X, an object field, and no CPY or mask on it has been found. Slots pointing at the same message: $9BC8 is named twice. That is in the data, not a parse error. Every one of the pointers lands on a message head, and the messages partition the block end to end - two statements from two directions, neither derived from the other.
